Subject: Dedicated capacity tierslab — options for GPU floor, burst & phased onramp (QuantaFlow)

Hi David,

Thanks for the call this morning — great to see the usage patterns you shared. Based on the 24/7 inference mix and the peak batch jobs in your weekly ETL window, I sketched three practical dedicated capacity options that map to different risk/reward and billing profiles. Attached is a spreadsheet with line-item pricing and an onramp diagram (qf_capacity_tiers_v3.xlsx, qf_onramp_diagram.png).

Summary (high-level):

Option A — Conservative floor (low up-front commitment)
- Cluster footprint: 8x A100-like GPUs (logical lanes)
- Min active GPUs: 4 (kept warm, pay reserved rate on those 4)
- Burst capacity: up to +50% (ephemeral burst pool billed at higher pay-as-you-go rate)
- Ramp: activate additional nodes at month 3 and month 6 as usage stabilizes
- SLA target: 99.9% availability for reserved lane

Option B — Growth-linked committed baseline (recommended for predictable throughput)
- Cluster footprint: 16x GPUs
- Min active GPUs: 12 (reserved)
- Burst: +100% for short windows (sustained bursts require brief warm-up)
- Ramp: staged activation: 50% day 1, +25% at month 2, +25% at month 4
- Includes priority routing and dedicated pre-warmed cache nodes

Option C — Aggressive reserved (lowest unit cost)
- Cluster footprint: 32x GPUs
- Min active GPUs: 24 (reserved)
- Burst: on demand up to 32x; includes longer warm pools for big-batch windows
- Ramp: immediate 70% activation, remaining 30% at month 2
- Best for teams centralizing heavy training-inference pipelines and batch re-ranking

Key operational notes:
- We manage prefix/KV cache warming for your hot models — saves ~20–30% token compute on average.
- We can attach a telemetry sample to your account for the first 30 days to tune batching/sequence length thresholds.
- Contract mechanics: monthly billing with a 12/24 month term option. Term-level discounts shown in spreadsheet.

Ask: please tell me which option best matches your tolerance for committed spend vs latency predictability and whether QuantaFlow needs the minimum active GPUs to be higher during your nightly ETL window. If you pick Option B we can lock a start date and prepare a DocuSign for the SOW/commitment.

Cheers,

Diego Fernandez

Diego,

Thanks — useful framing. A couple quick clarifications before we run this internally: 

1) For Option B: when you say "Min active GPUs: 12 (reserved)", does that mean we are billed for 12 GPUs continuously even if our baseline average is ~8 GPUs? We need clarity on how billing vs. activation works.

2) Burst semantics: our ETL window (daily, 02:00–04:00 PT) can spike for 30–60 minutes to ~28 GPUs. Can we guarantee that burst will ramp to that level within the first 10 minutes of the window without significant cold-start latency?

3) If we choose Option A today but then decide to move to Option B in month 2, what is the process and any proration/penalties?

Also, curious if you have an example SLA exception process — our security team will want a description of failover and fallback to hosted model variants in another region.

If you can reply with those three clarifications (billing behavior, burst warm-up, onramp/proration) I can share with my CFO and Ops.

—David

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity tierslab — options for GPU floor, burst & phased onramp (QuantaFlow)

David — good questions. Short answers first, details below.

1) Billing / Min active GPUs
- Reserved billing model: you are invoiced for the contracted "min active GPUs" at the reserved tier rate (discounted). Any additional ephemeral burst GPUs are billed at the pay-as-you-go burst rate.
- Practically: Option B would bill for 12 reserved GPUs each month. If your steady-state usage averages 8 GPUs, you still pay the reserved rate for 12; however, we can schedule an initial 30-day telemetry review and recommend cost/usage optimizations (cache tuning, quantization profile changes) to reduce that gap.

2) Burst warm-up and latency guarantees
- For 30–60 minute spikes to ~28 GPUs during your nightly ETL, we offer two mechanisms:
  a) Ephemeral burst pool: immediate capacity from shared burst nodes (typical ramp 0–10 minutes, depends on model KV cache warm-up)
  b) Warm-sliced burst lanes: we can allocate a small warm pool of pre-warmed instances (kept at higher cost) to guarantee sub-90s ramp (recommended for your ETL).
- Recommended for QuantaFlow: Option B + warm-sliced burst (pre-warmed 8 GPUs) achieves predictable < 90s ramp to 28 GPUs in our tests. We outline warm-slice costs in the spreadsheet.

3) Onramp / proration / switching
- Moving from Option A → B mid-term: we can offer a single mid-term amendment. Billing for newly reserved capacity begins on the amendment effective date; we prorate the reserved fee for the month. No early-termination penalty beyond the remaining committed term if you choose to reduce later — reductions are subject to a 30-day notice and may carry a modest step-down fee (documented in SOW).

SLA & failover
- Primary SLA: 99.9% regional availability for reserved lanes; 99.5% including burst capacity.
- Failover pattern: traffic routing policies automatically route to pre-configured fallback variants (hosted or cross-region dedicated) based on policy thresholds. For security sign-off we will provide a runbook + example incident timeline (we've attached a sample incident report template in the drive link).

Next steps
- If this all looks good, pick Option A/B/C and indicate whether you want warm-sliced burst capacity included in the SOW. We will generate an amendment and DocuSign for the SOW (Deal QF-2026-448).

Thanks,

Diego Fernandez
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
Attachments referenced: qf_capacity_tiers_v3.xlsx
